transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-21 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM), Maya Chen (Veridian Eng Lead), Ivan Kostov (Veridian Platform), Priya Rao (Veridian Security)

Summary (auto): quick hosted onramp demo focusing on streaming, params and retry behaviors; security and benchmarking next steps noted.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for carving time today, uh, we'll do a quick onramp to our hosted chat API, focus on streaming behavior, the parameters you asked about, and the retry story, and then leave time for the security questions. Maya thanks for coordinating.
[00:14] Maya (Veridian): yeah thanks, quick note - our primary concerns are latency under 250ms p95 for interactive flows, costs that don't blow up during spikes, and clear guardrails for PHI — so we'll ask about KMS and retention.
[00:28] Samira (Redwood SE): cool, that's helpful. quick map — we'll demo a streaming chat call first from the sandbox, cover tuneable params (temp, top_p, max_tokens), show the streaming chunk shape, then show retry/backoff patterns and how to do idempotency.
[00:44] Ivan (Veridian): can you show what streaming looks like client-side vs the full response? we have a websocket-based UI.
[00:58] Samira: yep; in hosted mode you can use server-sent events or websockets; the API streams delta tokens, and you get partial output as it generates. important: in heavy load we surface partial chunks and then a final completion event. here's a demo — starting a call...
[01:20] [audio glitch] Samira: ...okay, there's a small noise on my mic. so the client will receive incremental pieces like {"delta":"The quick"} then {"delta":" brown fox"} and so on. most clients append deltas.
[01:38] Maya: and what's the expected latency per first token for a short prompt?
[01:46] Samira: depends a lot on model + sequence length + batching. for our curated small chat models you should see first-token in ~80-140ms on our hosted tier in US-East under normal load. p95 varies — which is why we recommend the benchmark.
[02:05] Priya (Veridian): you said "curated small chat models" — do you mean quantized variants? do you do quantization in the hosted offering?
[02:15] Alex: yes, some of our catalog models are quantized and Redwood verifies perf profiles. on hosted you get the model variants we host; Dedicated/Private can be used if you need a specific binary or quantization profile.
[02:31] Ivan: how do retries look? if a request times out, what's the right client-side pattern?
[02:39] Samira: good question. we recommend idempotency keys for any non-idempotent flows; retries should be exponential backoff with jitter. typical pattern: try once, then backoff 200-500ms, then 1s, then 2s, stop after 3 retries. for streaming, if the connection drops mid-stream we provide resume tokens in some cases, but often the client will re-issue with the same idempotency key and the server will return the last completed chunk or a cached completion when available.
[03:10] Maya: resume tokens — is that explicit in the API or more internal?
[03:16] Samira: it's somewhat internal but we expose a resume_hint field for some models; it's not guaranteed across all variants. for guaranteed behavior pin a model version and use prefix caching — that gives much better cache hit rates.
[03:33] Alex: to add, our Console shows per-token cost and latency breakdowns, which helps you tune batch sizes vs cost. we'll share a short Console tour after.
[03:46] Jordan (Redwood CSM): and for the POC we usually instrument with sample prompts that mirror your UI and record p50/p95/p99 latencies + token costs, so you can compare Hosted vs Dedicated numbers.
[04:02] Maya: sounds good. one thing — we have strict PHI rules. can you quickly run through your KMS and retention story?
[04:11] Alex: sure. Hosted default: ephemeral keys managed by Redwood, we store request metadata and model outputs per your retention window. for customers needing more control, Dedicated offers customer-managed KMS integration and Private allows you to bring your own HSM. we'll send the SOC2 + KMS integration doc.
[04:30] Priya: do you support SSO + RBAC for Console?
[04:34] Jordan: yes SSO via SAML/OIDC, role-based access controls in Console, audit logs in Dedicated/Private with longer retention for enterprise tiers.
[04:44] Ivan: okay good. back to retries — can you show an example of a retry-friendly request payload?
[04:50] Samira: sure, here's an example: include an idempotency_token at the top level, make sure your client persists it for retries. also set a reasonable max_tokens and a streaming timeout on the client so you don't create ghost requests.
[05:05] [20s silence while Samira pulls up sample code]
[05:25] Samira: all right, demoing a short prompt — params: temperature 0.2, max_tokens 64, streaming true. watch the SSE frames come in.
[05:36] [SSE frames audible in demo]
[05:38] Maya: okay I can see the incremental chunks. if there's an early stop because of safety filters, what's the client behavior?
[05:48] Samira: we'll send a final event with a safety flag and error code; client should treat that as a valid completion and show a soft fail message. for more control you can set moderation toggles; also the Console surfaces content safety incidents.
[06:04] Priya: about data residency — our customers in EU require data not to leave region. do you support region pinning on Hosted?
[06:12] Alex: yes region routing is supported; hosted can pin to EU regions. for strict residency we often recommend Private.
[06:20] Ivan: can we talk about batching? we have very chatty UI and want to understand throughput vs latency tradeoffs.
[06:27] Samira: batching improves throughput and reduces per-token cost but increases first-token latency. our Optimize tool analyzes traces and suggests batching windows. for interactive chat we typically keep micro-batch windows under 50-100ms to avoid perceptible lag.
[06:44] Maya: micro-batching? do you do async micro-batching client-side or server-side?
[06:50] Samira: server-side. client sends requests as usual; runtime will form batches based on policy. you can influence this via routing hints and priority flags.
[07:04] Alex: quick interjection — one common pattern: send short prompts with a small cacheable prefix and rely on prefix caching for common system prompts, which reduces compute.
[07:12] Maya: ok that's useful. now if we switch to Dedicated later, what changes in API?
[07:18] Samira: API surface stays the same; config flags differ for autoscaling and you get private networking. the Console shows Dedicated capacity metrics and you can pin kernels or quantization profiles in Dedicated/Private.
[07:33] Priya: audit logs — is there a way to get token-level redaction in the logs? we cannot store raw PHI in plaintext logs.
[07:41] Jordan: you can enable token redaction and set redaction policies; for full compliance we recommend Private with customer-side redaction before sending.
[07:53] Maya: great. one of our product folks asked about stop sequences — we sometimes need deterministic endings. any advice?
[07:59] Samira: combine stop sequences with a conservative max_tokens and low temperature; also use top_p truncation. if determinism is critical, set temperature 0 and pin to a smaller model.
[08:15] Ivan: request volumes — we have diurnal spikes, say 10x in the evenings. how does Hosted handle bursting?
[08:22] Alex: hosted supports burst capacity but subject to tenant limits; Dedicated gives predictable units. for spikes we recommend a fallback policy to a cheaper model or a lower-fidelity variant to keep latency SLOs.
[08:36] Maya: can you show the Console view for route fallback and cost dashboards?
[08:40] Alex: quick screen share of Console — here's per-route tokens, latency histograms, and a fallback policy config. you can set thresholds so if p95 latency > 300ms route to a cheaper model.
[08:57] [screen share continues]
[09:10] Priya: if you route to cheaper model mid-conversation, how do you keep context consistent?
[09:16] Samira: model variants must be architecture-compatible; we do semantic similarity checks before automatic fallbacks. Console shows compatibility and you can set hard/soft fallbacks.
[09:30] Maya: okay good. what about pricing — do you price Hosted per-token? what's the delta for streaming vs sync?
[09:37] Alex: hosted is per-token; streaming doesn't change unit pricing, but you might see different cost due to model choice and pre-token overhead. Dedicated pricing is capacity-based. we'll send a tailored sheet for your volume bands.
[09:54] Ivan: on metrics for the POC, what should we collect?
[09:59] Jordan: collect p50/p95/p99 latencies, token counts per session, model version, and error rates. we'll instrument trace ids to join logs.
[10:10] Maya: can Redwood ingest our synthetic workload? we can export a replay.
[10:15] Samira: yes we can run replay on our staging infra; that's actually the best way to get realistic numbers. please send sample prompts and concurrency profile.
[10:24] Maya: will do.
[10:28] [brief pause]
[10:34] Ivan: a small nit — We're concerned about reconnect storms if a mobile client reconnects a lot. any recommended client patterns?
[10:41] Samira: implement jittered backoff, exponential with cap, and avoid aggressive polling. also include lightweight health checks to detect flooding. Console can emit alerts on reconnect rates.
[10:53] Priya: about KMS: can we envelope-encrypt at client side before sending?
[10:58] Alex: yes you can pre-encrypt sensitive fields; however model can't operate on encrypted inputs. typical approach is to tokenize or pseudonymize before sending, or run in Private where data never leaves your network.
[11:18] Maya: okay let's talk POC success criteria. Our bar: p95 <= 250ms for main chat flow, average cost per session under $0.03, and no safety incidents for our test set. can Redwood commit to instrumenting these?
[11:31] Jordan: yes, we'll capture those metrics in the pilot and set up a shared dashboard.
[11:36] Alex: next, a short walkthrough on parameter tuning — temperature, top_p, top_k, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty.
[11:45] Samira: examples: temperature 0.0-0.2 for deterministic; 0.6+ for creative. top_p at 0.9 gives a narrow nucleus. frequency/presence penalties help reduce repetition. also, shorter max_tokens reduces cost.
[12:03] Maya: about stop sequences again — our UI has buttons that expect JSON outputs; is structured output supported?
[12:10] Samira: yes you can use structured output prompts and Redwood supports tool-calling and JSON-schema constraints on some models. Console also validates generated JSON in some flows.
[12:22] Ivan: how hard is it to switch model versions mid-POC? we may want to try two models back-to-back.
[12:28] Samira: trivial from API perspective — specify model parameter. watch out for differences in tokenization which can change token counts; Console compares tokenization delta.
[12:40] [demo shows model switch]
[12:50] Maya: good. final question on retries — do retries duplicate cost if the first attempt succeeded but the ack got lost?
[12:58] Samira: yes, duplicates can cost tokens. that's why idempotency keys and server-side dedup are important. with idempotency if the server already completed the request we'll return cached result rather than re-executing. but cache hit depends on cache TTL and request fingerprinting.
[13:18] Ivan: okay that helps. for the benchmark, what hooks do you need from us?
[13:23] Samira: sample prompt set, concurrency targets, desired region, and any required redaction/pseudonymization rules. we'll run on hosted staging and share raw traces.
[13:33] Maya: we'll prepare that.
[13:36] Alex: last bit — we'll also share a short playbook: recommended client settings for web and mobile, and a retry policy template.
[13:45] Priya: please do. also include the security whitepaper.
[13:48] Alex: will do.
[13:50] Jordan: recap of next steps: Alex shares pricing + security docs, Samira runs the 48-hour benchmark, Jordan sends pilot success template.
[13:59] Maya: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[14:02] Alex: thanks, we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the POC kickoff pending the benchmark.
[14:08] [call ends]
